extracted.intended_audience: people typesetting mathematics with TeX (authors, editors, advanced users)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and low-level rules for producing high-quality mathematical typesetting in TeX (plain TeX/LaTeX). Covers delimiter usage, math-mode punctuation, font families, math atom/class behavior, generalized fractions, and debugging tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pairing rule for \left and \right
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever you use \left and \right they must pair up with each other, just as braces do in groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You cannot have a \left in one formula and the matching \right in another, nor can you cross groups (e.g., ‘\left(...{...\right)...}’ or ‘\left(...\begingroup...\right)...\endgroup’). This is because TeX must typeset the enclosed subformula to decide delimiter size.

rubrics_metrics.name: \left/\right act as grouping (local scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: \left and \right perform grouping in addition to making delimiters; any definitions made between them are local as if braces surrounded the subformula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions inside a \left...\right region are local to that region (like a group). This affects scoping of font/parameter changes etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit-delimiter sizing preferred in special situations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use \bigl, \bigr, \Biggl, \bigg, etc., when \left and \right choose sizes that are too small or too large, or when you must match sizes across broken displays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three typical cases: (1) \left/\right choose a smaller delimiter than you want (e.g., nested absolute-value differences); (2) they choose a larger delimiter than desired (commonly when enclosing large operators with limits, where letting the limits 'hang out' looks better—use \bigg etc.); (3) when splitting a very large displayed formula across lines and you want identical opening/closing sizes, use explicit sizes on each line (e.g., \Biggl ... \Biggr) because \left and \right must be paired on the same line/formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of null delimiter (\left. or \right.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Typing '.' after \left or \right specifies a null (invisible) delimiter, useful when only one visible delimiter is needed (e.g., piecewise brace with no matching visible brace).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A null delimiter is not empty: it is an empty box whose width is the TeX parameter \nulldelimiterspace (plain TeX sets it to 1.2pt). Example: to produce a left brace with no visible right brace, use '\left\{ ... \right.'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Angle-bracket shorthand
rubrics_metrics.description: You can type '<' or '>' as convenient abbreviations for \langle and \rangle when TeX is looking for a delimiter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that '<' and '>' normally produce the less-than/greater-than relations, not angle brackets; the shorthand works only when TeX is in a delimiter-choosing context (e.g., after \left or explicit delimiter commands).

rubrics_metrics.name: Special delimiter commands available
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain TeX provides additional delimiters like \arrowvert, \Arrowvert, \bracevert, \lgroup, \rgroup, \lmoustache, \rmoustache, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These produce delimiters built from repeatable parts (arrow shafts, brace halves, etc.). Note: \lgroup and \rgroup exist only in large sizes (\Big or larger) and cannot be used exactly like parentheses in all contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subscript/superscript behavior after delimiters
rubrics_metrics.description: The placement/attachment of a following subscript or superscript depends on the delimiter command used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After a \left delimiter, the first subscript/superscript belongs to the enclosed subformula (effectively preceded by {}); after a \right delimiter, a following sub/sup is attached to the entire \left...\right subformula; after a \bigl or \bigr (or \bigm, \big) the sub/sup applies only to that specific delimiter. Example: '\bigl(_2' vs '\left(_2' behave differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delimiter sizing algorithm parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX computes delimiter sizes based on the vertical extents of the enclosed subformula and two parameters: \delimiterfactor (f) and \delimitershortfall (δ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the enclosed subformula extends y1 above axis and y2 below, let y = 2·max(y1,y2). The minimum delimiter size is at least y·f/1000 and at least y − δ. Plain TeX uses f=901 and δ=5pt (Appendix B). This explains why \left/\right choose particular sizes and why explicit sizing may be preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: When \left/\right may choose undesirable sizes (enclosing operators)
rubrics_metrics.description: \left and \right cause delimiters to enclose large operators together with their limits, which can lead to visually awkward large delimiters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a large operator with limits (e.g., \sum with limits) appears, consider using explicit large delimiters (\biggl, \biggr, \Biggl, etc.) so limits 'hang out' and typography looks better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use explicit paired sizes to match delimiters across broken displays
rubrics_metrics.description: Because \left and \right must occur in the same formula, they cannot be used across multiple lines; to ensure matching opening/closing sizes across split displays, use matching explicit-size commands (e.g., \Biggl ... \Biggr).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When breaking a large displayed formula into two or more lines and you want identical delimiter sizes at start/end, pick an explicit size on each line rather than relying on \left/\right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of delimiter variant availability and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Delimiters (including slashes and angle brackets) have maximum available sizes; for some symbols extremely large sizes may be capped at the largest available glyph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: \left/\right can make arbitrarily large delimiters (bigger than \big... commands) but some symbols have a maximum size; TeX will use the largest available variant for those symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \vcenter to center material vertically with respect to the math axis
rubrics_metrics.description: To create a box that is vertically centered about the math axis, use \vcenter{...} (only legal in math mode).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you need to center something vertically in horizontal mode, put it in math mode: '$\vcenter{...}$'. Constructions like '\vcenter to <dimen>' and '\vcenter spread <dimen>' are also legal. \vcenter packs vertical-mode material as if by \vbox and then raises/lowers it so top edge is as far above axis as bottom edge is below.

rubrics_metrics.name: You can insert any box into math mode with \hbox/\vbox/\vtop/\box/\copy
rubrics_metrics.description: Boxes produced by these commands behave like ordinary symbols when inserted into formulas; you can also use \raise, \lower, \vrule inside math mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such constructions produce atoms (e.g., Ord or Vcent) and are useful for ad-hoc or single-use symbols; for general macros consider style-dependent constructions (\mathchoice/\mathpalette).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \mathchoice for style-dependent symbol choices (but it's expensive)
rubrics_metrics.description: \mathchoice{display}{text}{script}{scriptscript} writes four alternatives; TeX chooses the appropriate one depending on current math style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TeX actually typesets all four alternatives before choosing, so \mathchoice is time/space expensive; use it only when necessary (e.g., for macros that must render differently in different math styles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \mathpalette to simplify \mathchoice-based macros
rubrics_metrics.description: \mathpalette is a helper for \mathchoice-style macros; '\mathpalette\a{xyz}' expands to a four-part \mathchoice that calls \a with the style selection as first argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appendix B shows examples (\phantom, \root, \smash). \mathpalette is convenient when defining macros whose behavior must depend on the math style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalized fractions and delimiter-aware forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Commands \over, \atop, \choose, \above are special cases of more general primitives: \overwithdelims, \atopwithdelims, \abovewithdelims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'withdelims' forms to specify left/right delimiters and fraction bar thickness. For example, \choose ≡ \atopwithdelims() and \over ≡ \overwithdelims.. (null delimiters). Use \abovewithdelims to specify explicit bar thickness. Selecting the right form controls delimiters and bar thickness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \mathchardef/\mathchar to define math symbols properly
rubrics_metrics.description: Math characters can be specified by numeric codes (class, family, position). \mathchardef provides a convenient way to assign control sequences to math characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., '\mathchardef\sum="1350' to define \sum. \mathchar and \delimiter number forms pack class/family/position information into hex numbers; these low-level tools are useful when constructing symbol definitions in formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize math fonts into families and set \textfont/\scriptfont/\scriptscriptfont
rubrics_metrics.description: All math characters belong to one of 16 families (0–15), each with three fonts (text, script, scriptscript). Use \textfont, \scriptfont, \scriptscriptfont to assign fonts for each family.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plain TeX assigns family 0 to roman (\tenrm/\sevenrm/\fiverm) and family 1 to math italics etc. Changes to \textfont etc. are local to groups. INITEX initializes mathcodes; you can use \newfam to allocate families. Families 2 and 3 must have fonts with certain \fontdimen parameters (cmsy, cmex).

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and use math classes (0–7) appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Each math character has a class 0–7: ordinary, large operator, binary, relation, opening, closing, punctuation, and family-dependent (class 7). Class controls spacing and grammar ('parts of speech' in math).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can force classes for subformulas using \mathord, \mathop, \mathbin, \mathrel, \mathopen, \mathclose, \mathpunct. Class 7 behaves like class 0 unless \fam is set to a legal family number; letters are usually class 7 so they follow the current \fam. Use \mathcode to change character behavior in math mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \delcode to control delimiter small/large variants
rubrics_metrics.description: Each character has a \delcode indicating small and large variants (six hex digits: three for small, three for large); negative delcode means not a delimiter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TeX consults \delcode when a character follows \left or \right, or one of the withdelims commands; if small/large variant is 000 that variant is ignored. Example: '\delcode`( = "028300' says small variant at position 028 of family 0 and large variant at position 300 of family 3. All delcodes start as -1 until changed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do punctuation for inline vs displayed math correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: When a formula is followed by a period, comma, semicolon, colon, question mark, exclamation point, etc., put the punctuation after the $ for inline formulas, but put the punctuation before the $$ for displayed formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example inline: 'If $x<0$, we have shown that ...' Example displayed: '... $$y=f(x).$$' This preserves correct interword spacing in paragraphs and avoids incorrect thin-space insertion. Also avoid constructions like 'for $x = a, b$, or $c$'; instead write 'for $x = a$, $b$, or $c$' or use a tie 'or~$c$'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep math properly segregated from surrounding sentence punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not include linguistic punctuation (commas, periods) that belong to the sentence inside math delimiters unless they are really part of the formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Putting sentence punctuation inside math can produce wrong spacing and inhibit line breaks (TeX won't break at spaces inside formulas as it would between words). Also don't take operators like '-' and '=' outside of $...$; keep operators inside math mode when they are part of the formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspect math lists with \showlists for debugging
rubrics_metrics.description: You can use \showlists in math mode to see TeX's internal representation of a math list (atoms, fields, families, etc.) in the log file.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The output uses prefixes (dots for hierarchy, '^' for superscript field, '_' for subscript). This is useful to understand how TeX is parsing your formula and to debug grouping, atom types, and font/family assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand math-list composition and atom kinds
rubrics_metrics.description: A math list is made of items such as atoms, horizontal/vertical material, glue, kerns, style changes, generalized fractions, boundaries, and math choices. Atoms have nucleus, superscript, subscript fields and come in 13 kinds (Ord, Op, Bin, Rel, Open, Close, Punct, Inner, Over, Under, Acc, Rad, Vcent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowing the internal structure (fields can be empty, a math symbol, a box, or a math list) helps when writing macros or debugging complex math constructions. For example, fractions and \left...\right are treated as \mathinner and receive additional spacing in certain contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: When defining macros for math, consider family/fam interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Class 7 math characters take their family from the parameter \fam (default -1 on entering math) so definitions like '\rm' change \fam to 0; this affects how letters are typeset in math mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you want bold math italics in a new family, set \fam appropriately in a wrapper (e.g., \bmit sets \fam=9) and define symbols so they respect \fam. Remember \fam is irrelevant in horizontal mode but crucial in math mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious with low-level numeric \mathchar and \delimiter codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Numeric conventions for \mathchar and \delimiter pack class/family/position (and small/large variants) into hex numbers and are compact but cryptic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These low-level primitives are used by formats to define symbols and delimiters; use them when creating format-level definitions but understand their semantics (e.g., leading hex digit is class for \mathchar; \delimiter can be up to 7 hex digits). Mistakes can produce errors or unexpected symbol behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Families 2 and 3 need fonts with special \fontdimen parameters for math spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX insists that fonts assigned to families 2 and 3 (ordinary math symbols and large symbols) provide certain \fontdimen parameters used by math spacing rules (Appendix G).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The cmsy and cmex symbol fonts are designed for these families; if you assign other fonts to families 2/3, ensure the necessary \fontdimen parameters exist or adjust spacing via \fontdimen.
